rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The divine ritual signs are marks of the rites: pilgrimage stations, pebble-throwing places, circumambulation, sa‘y, and acts marking the pilgrim’s state and worship.
rows.anchor: اسم لما أشعر أى جعل شعارا وعلامة للنسك من مواقف الحج ومرامى الجمار والطواف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Attributing the rites to God honors them and makes the gravity of declaring them lawful unmistakable; the prohibition guards their sanctity and pilgrims’ observance.
rows.anchor: وإضافتها إلى الله تعالى لتشريفها وتهويل الخطب فى احلالها

rows.speaker: عطاء
rows.claim: ʿAṭāʾ explains the divine signs as God’s limits, commands, prohibitions, and obligations.
rows.anchor: روى عن عطاء أنه فسر الشعائر بما لم حدود الله تعالى وأمره ونهيه وفرضه

rows.speaker: أبو علي الجبائي
rows.claim: Abū ʿAlī al-Jubbāʾī takes the signs as markers distinguishing lawful territory from the sanctuary; violating them means entering Mecca without consecration.
rows.anchor: أن المراد بها العلامات المنصوبة للفرق بين الحل والحرم ومعنى إحلالها عنده مجاوزتها إلى مكة بغير إحرام

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid is reported to identify the signs with al-Ṣafā, al-Marwa, sacrificial camels, and other such rites.
rows.anchor: وقيل : هى الصفا والمروة والهدى من البدن وغيرها وروى ذلك عن مجاهد

rows.speaker: ابن عباس، قتادة
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās and Qatāda interpret not making the sacred month lawful as refraining from fighting polytheist enemies during it.
rows.anchor: بأن تقاتلوا فيه أعدائكم من المشركين كما روى عن ابن عباس وقتادة

rows.speaker: القتيبي
rows.claim: Al-Qutaybī offers another interpretation: declaring the sacred month lawful by postponing it through nasīʾ.
rows.anchor: أو بالنسىء كما نقل عن القتيبى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ālūsī prefers the prohibition on fighting in the sacred month as more fitting for the believers addressed.
rows.anchor: والأول هو الأولى بحال المؤمنين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The month is variously identified as Rajab, Dhū al-Qaʿdah, or all four sacred months; the last is preferred by al-Jubbāʾī and al-Balkhī, with the singular used generically.
rows.anchor: الأشهر الاربعة الحرم واختاره الجبائى والبلخى وإفراده لإرادة الجنس

rows.speaker: عكرمة
rows.claim: ʿIkrima is specifically reported to identify the sacred month as Dhū al-Qaʿdah.
rows.anchor: ذوالقعدة وروى ذلك عن عكرمة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sacrificial offering must not be seized or prevented from reaching its place; it includes camels, cattle, and sheep dedicated to the Kaʿba.
rows.anchor: بأن يعترض له بالغضب أو بالمنع من أن يبلغ محله والمراد به مايهدى إلى الكعبة من إبل أو بقر أو شاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The offering is singled out despite belonging to the ritual signs because it benefits people, is property that may be treated carelessly, and is among the greatest rites.
rows.anchor: للناس ولأنه مالى قد يتساهل فيه وتعظيما له لأنه من أعظمها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Collars made from sandals, tree bark, or similar material mark an offering so it will not be molested; the prohibition primarily protects the collared offerings.
rows.anchor: وهى مايقلد به الهدى من نعل أو لحاء شجر أو غيرهما ليعلم أنه هدى فلا يتعرض له

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wording can also prohibit touching the collars themselves, by an a fortiori analogy with the ban on displaying adornments in 24:31, which implies protecting their concealed locations too.
rows.anchor: ولايبدين زينتهن فانهن إذا نهين عن إظهار الزينة كالخلخال والسوار

rows.speaker: أبو علي الجبائي، الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Jubbāʾī, with the view also transmitted from al-Ḥasan, says the command forbids treating the collars themselves as lawful and requires giving them in charity when valuable.
rows.anchor: أبى على الجبائى أن المراد النهى عن إحلال نفس القلائد وإيجاب التصدق بها ان كانت لها قيمة وروى ذلك عن الحسن

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: Al-Suddī says “the collars” means the owners of offerings: Arabs marked themselves and their camels with Meccan bark after the sacred months to travel home safely.
rows.anchor: وروى عن السدى أن المراد من القلائد أصحاب الهدى فن العرب كانوا يقلدون من لحاء شجر مكة

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farrāʾ distinguishes the practice: sanctuary residents wore collars of bark, while people from outside used wool, hair, and similar materials.
rows.anchor: أهل الحرم كانوا يتقلدون بلحاء الشجر وغير أهل الحرم كانوا يتقلدون بالصوف والشعر

rows.speaker: الربيع، عطاء
rows.claim: Al-Rabīʿ and ʿAṭāʾ understand the verse to forbid believers from removing sanctuary trees to make collars, a practice of the polytheists in pre-Islamic times.
rows.anchor: وعن الربيع وعطاء أن المراد نهى المؤمنين أن ينزعوا شيئا من شجر الحرم يقلدون به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse forbids harming or turning away anyone headed for the Sacred House; “fighting a people” or “harming a people” may be understood with an omitted noun.
rows.anchor: أى ولاتحلوا أقواما قاصدين البيت الحرام بأن تصدوهم عنه بأى وجه كان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A reading has “wa-lā āmmī al-bayta” in an annexation construction, with “the House” as the object of the active participle rather than an adverbial destination.
rows.anchor: وقرىء ولا آمى البيت الحرام بالاضافة والبيت مفعول به لا ظرف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Seeking bounty and approval” is a circumstantial clause attached to the implicit subject of “those heading”; it may be an adjective, though that weakens the active participle’s ability to govern.
rows.anchor: حال من المستكن فى آمين وجوز أن يكون صفة وضعف بأن اسم الفاعل الموصوف لايعمل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The adjective analysis is defended when its complement follows the adjective, since delayed complements can remain governed after the construction is complete.
rows.anchor: بأن الوصف إنما يمنع من العمل إذا تقدم المعمول فلو تأخر لم يمنع لمجيئه بعد الفراغ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The indefinite “bounty” and “approval” magnify them; “from their Lord” modifies the seeking or describes the bounty, while the possessive Lord-language honors them and signals fulfillment of their aim.
rows.anchor: من ربهم متعلق بنفس العمل أو بمحذوف وقع صفة لفضلا مغنية عن وصف ماعطف عليه بها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One interpretation takes those heading for the sanctuary as believers alone and regards the verse as un-abrogated; an objection is that harming Muslims is forbidden whether or not they are pilgrims.
rows.anchor: والمراد بهم المسلمون خاصة والآية محكمة

rows.speaker: الحسن وغيره
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan and others take those heading for the sanctuary as polytheists; “bounty” then means their trade profit and “approval” what they claim to seek.
rows.anchor: المراد بالآمين هم المشركون خاصة والمراد من الفضل حينئذ الربح فى تجارتهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Even on the polytheist reading, bounty and approval may retain their real meanings; al-Ālūsī prefers that since the wording can bear what is true in reality.
rows.anchor: لما أمكن حمله على ماهو فى نفس الأمر كان حمله عليه أولى يؤيد هذا القول

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: Al-Suddī links the revelation to al-Ḥuṭaym ibn Hind of Banū Rabīʿa, who feigned interest in Islam, then raided the city’s herd and made the stolen animals offerings; the Muslims were stopped from pursuing him.
rows.anchor: فى رجل من بنى ربيعة يقال له الحطيم بن هند وذلك أنه أتى إلى النبى

rows.speaker: ابن زيد
rows.claim: Ibn Zayd says the verse came at the conquest of Mecca when Muslims wanted to attack polytheist horsemen approaching the House for ʿumra.
rows.anchor: وروى عن ابن زيد أنها نزلت يوم فتح مكة فى فوارس يؤمون البيت من المشركين

rows.speaker: ابن جريج
rows.claim: Ibn Jurayj denies abrogation, reasoning that Muslims may initiate combat against polytheists during the sacred months; al-Ālūsī objects that the verse is not explicit about fighting.
rows.anchor: ابن جريج أنه لانسخ لأنه يجوز أن يبتدىء المشركون فى الأشهر الحرم بالقتال

rows.speaker: أبو مسلم
rows.claim: Abū Muslim holds that the prohibition concerning those heading to the sanctuary was abrogated by the command that polytheists not approach the Sacred Mosque after that year.
rows.anchor: إن الآية منسوخة بقوله تعالى : فلايقريبوا المسجد الحرام بعد عامهم هذا

rows.speaker: قائلون بالنسخ
rows.claim: Other exegetes say the verse was abrogated by the sword verse, or by both it and the prohibition on approaching the mosque.
rows.anchor: وقيل : بآية السيف وقيل : بهما

rows.speaker: ابن أبي نجيح، مجاهد
rows.claim: A report through Ibn Abī Najīḥ from Mujāhid says that only the clause about collars was abrogated.
rows.anchor: لم ينسخ من هذه الآية إلا القلائد وروى ذلك عن ابن أبى نجيح عن مجاهد

rows.speaker: قائلون بالعموم
rows.claim: Some hold that those heading to the House include Muslims and polytheists: a specific occasion does not restrict general wording, though abrogation applies only to polytheists.
rows.anchor: المراد بالآمين مايعم المسلمين والمشركين وخصوص السبب لايمنع عموم اللفظ والنسخ حينئذ فى حق المشركين خاصة

rows.speaker: حميد بن قيس الأعرج
rows.claim: Ḥumayd ibn Qays al-Aʿraj reads “tabtaghūn” with second-person address, making the clause describe the believers’ state and its incompatibility with the forbidden conduct, not condition the ban.
rows.anchor: وقرأ حميد بن قيس الأعرج تبتغون بالتاء على خطاب المؤمنين والجملة على ذلك حال من ضمير المخاطبين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The address reading is challenged because believers would more naturally be told “your Lord”; the reply says “their Lord” warns that God protects them and will not approve the assault, and also stresses God is Lord of all.
rows.anchor: واعترض بأنه لو أريد خطاب المؤمنين لكان المناسب من ربكم وربهم وأجيب بأن ترك التعبير بما ذكر للتخويف

rows.speaker: شيخ الإسلام
rows.claim: Shaykh al-Islām says the possessive “their Lord” in the address reading signals honor reserved for the pilgrims and deprivation of the addressees from that honor and their sought aim.
rows.anchor: إن اضافة الرب إلى ضمير آمين على قراءة الخطاب للايماء إلى اقتصار التشريف عليهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “When you emerge from consecration” refers back to “while you are consecrated” in 5:1; hunting is then permitted because its impediment has ended.
rows.anchor: أى فلا جناح عليكم بالاصطياد لزوال المانع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command to hunt after consecration exemplifies an imperative of permission following a prohibition, a common view among jurists and theologians.
rows.anchor: وإلى كون الأمر للإباحة بعد الحظر كثير

rows.speaker: صاحب القواطع، ابن برهان
rows.claim: The permission reading is the apparent position of al-Shāfiʿī and is reported by Ibn Burhān from most jurists and theologians.
rows.anchor: إنه ظاهر كلام الشافعى فى أحكام القرآن ونقله ابن برهان عن أكثر الفقهاء والمتكلمين

rows.speaker: القاضي أبو الطيب، أبو إسحاق، السمعاني، الإمام في المحصول
rows.claim: A second legal-theoretical position says the imperative remains obligatory because its form entails obligation and the prior prohibition does not alter it.
rows.anchor: ثانيها أنه للوجوب لأن الصيغة تقتضيه ووروده بعد الحظر لاتأثير له

rows.speaker: إمام الحرمين
rows.claim: Imām al-Ḥaramayn suspends judgment between permission and obligation for commands following prohibitions.
rows.anchor: وثالثها الوقف بينهما وهو قول إمام الحرمين

rows.speaker: الزركشي
rows.claim: Al-Zarkashī suggests that the legal status might return to what it was before the prohibition, as some argue about a prohibition following a command.
rows.anchor: أن يقال هنا برجوع الحال إلى مكان قبل كما قيل فى مسألة النهى الوارد بعد الوجوب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those treating the imperative as literally obligatory explain it as rhetorical emphasis on how fully permissible hunting is.
rows.anchor: إن حقيقة الأمر المذكور للايجاب قال إنه مبالغة فى صحة المباح حتى كأنه واجب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The suggestion that the command requires belief in permissibility is rejected as an unsound figurative reading of the object.
rows.anchor: إن الأمر فى مثله لوجوب اعتقاد الحل فيكون التجوز فى المادة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Aḥlaltum” is also read as a dialectal variant of “ḥalaltum.”
rows.anchor: وقرىء أحللتم وهو لغة فى حل

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan is reported to read “fa-ṣṭādū” with a kasra transferred from the elided hamza; grammarians object that transfer onto a vowel conflicts with the regular pattern, while another explanation hears imāla rather than a pure kasra.
rows.anchor: وعن الحسن أنه قرىء فاصطادوا بكسر الفاء بنقل حركة همزة الوصل عليها وضعفت من جهة العربية

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatāda glosses “yajrimannakum” as “make you” or “cause you,” a usage supported by a cited line where the deed caused Fazāra to become angry.
rows.anchor: لايحملنكم كما فسره به قتادة ونقل عن ثعلب والكسائى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The cited verse says the deed caused Fazāra to become angry; on this analysis the verb takes one object directly and the other with “ʿalā.”
rows.anchor: جرمت فزارة بعدها أن تغضبا فجرم على هذا يتعدى لواحد بنفسه وإلى الآخر بعلى

rows.speaker: الفراء، أبو عبيدة
rows.claim: Al-Farrāʾ and Abū ʿUbayda gloss the verb as “earn” or “bring upon”; it patterns like kasaba in taking one or two objects, but usually concerns harmful earnings, fitting this warning.
rows.anchor: المعنى لايكسبنكم وجرم جار مجرى كسب فى المعنى والتعدى إلى مفعول واحد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The root originally suggests cutting off, since an earner devotes himself to the earning; “crime” accordingly became associated with harmful earning.
rows.anchor: لمعنى القطع لأن الكاسب ينقطع لكسبه

rows.speaker: عبد الله
rows.claim: A reading attributed to ʿAbd Allāh has “yujrimannakum” with the initial yāʾ in ḍamma.
rows.anchor: قراءة عبد الله لايجرمنكم بضم الياء

rows.speaker: ابن عامر، أبو بكر عن عاصم، إسماعيل عن نافع
rows.claim: Ibn ʿĀmir, Abū Bakr from ʿĀṣim, and Ismāʿīl from Nāfiʿ read “shanʾān” with a quiescent nūn; both this and the vowelled form may be verbal nouns or adjectives.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن عامر وأبوبكر عن عاصم وإسماعيل عن نافع بسكونها وفيهما احتمالان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: As a verbal noun, “shanʾān” means hatred or its intensity; the forms are irregular for a transitive verb and for a non-motion sense.
rows.anchor: يكونا مصدرين بمعنى البغض أو شدته شذوذا لأن فغلان بالفتح مصدر مايدل على الحركة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If adjectival, “shanʾān” means detested; the annexation is explanatory rather than a subject or object relation.
rows.anchor: يكونا صفتين لأن فعلان فى الصفات كثير كسكران

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If it is a verbal noun, the annexation most naturally makes the people its object, though it may instead make them the subject; al-Ālūsī calls the first analysis more apparent.
rows.anchor: فالظاهر أن اضافته إلى المفعول أى تبغضوا قوما وجوز أن تكون إلى الفاعل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: With the fatḥa reading, “because they barred you” is causal, referring to al-Ḥudaybiyya; with the kasra reading of Ibn Kathīr and Abū ʿAmr, it is conditional.
rows.anchor: بفتح الهمزة بتقدير اللام على أنه علة للشنآ ن أى لأن صدوكم عام الحديبية وقرأ ابن كثير وأبو عمرو بكسر الهمزة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although one objects that no one barred Muslims after the conquest, the wording can mean they had barred them before or warn against revenge even after Islam’s victory.
rows.anchor: إن كانوا قد صدوكم وأن يكون على ظاهره إشارة إلى أنه لاينبغى أن يجرمنكم شنآن قوم

rows.speaker: شيخ الإسلام
rows.claim: Shaykh al-Islām takes “barred you from the Sacred Mosque” as barring visitation and circumambulation for ʿumra; he calls this clear evidence that those heading there include polytheists, while others use it to limit the phrase to them.
rows.anchor: أى عن زيارته والطواف به للعمرة وهذه كما قال شيخ الاسلام آية بينة فى عموم آمين للمشركين قطعا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “That you aggress” means aggress against them; the object is omitted because context supplies it, emphasizing restraint by the addressees and preservation of the rites rather than concern for the targets.
rows.anchor: أى عليهم وحذف تعويلا على الظهور وإيماءا إلى أن المقصد الأصلى منع صدور الاعتداء من المخاطبين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Whether “that you aggress” follows an omitted preposition or is the second object of “cause,” the verse forbids hatred over their prior barring from prompting assault or revenge.
rows.anchor: لايحملنكم بغض قوم لصدهم اياكم عن المسجد الحرام على اعتدائكم عليهم وانتقامكم منهم للتشفى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse truly forbids the addressees’ aggression; forbidding the causes and beginnings of an act forbids the act itself by demonstrative reasoning.
rows.anchor: فان النهى عن اسباب الشىء ومباديه المؤدية اليه نهى عنه بالطريق البرهانى وإبطال للسببية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The position of the hunting permission before this ban evokes pilgrims in consecration as game near the sanctuary; after they leave consecration, they may be approached like lawful game.
rows.anchor: بين ماتقدم وبين هذا النهى المتعلق به ليكون إشارة وإدماجا إلى أن القاصدين ماداموا محرمين مبتغين فضلا من ربهم كانوا كالصيد عند الحرم

rows.speaker: شيخ الإسلام
rows.claim: Shaykh al-Islām explains the delayed prohibition as showing that the ban on aggression outlasts consecration, unlike the hunting ban, and protects other pilgrims a fortiori until their connection to the rites ends.
rows.anchor: لعل تأخير هذا النهى عن ذلك مع ظهور تعلقه بما قبله للايذان بأن حرمة الاعتداء لاتنتهى بالخروج عن الاحرام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The exhortation to cooperate in righteousness is semantically attached to the ban on aggression: do not retaliate against pilgrims who barred you; instead, forgive and overlook.
rows.anchor: عطف على ولايجرمنكم من حيث المعنى كأنه قيل : لاتعتدوا على قاصدى المسجد الحرام لأجل أن صددتم عنه وتعاونوا على العفو والاغضاء

rows.speaker: قائلون بالاستئناف
rows.claim: Some treat “cooperate in righteousness” as a new sentence and require a full stop after “that you aggress.”
rows.anchor: هو استئناف والوقف ععلى أن تعتدوا لازم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other scholars make righteousness general obedience to command and God-consciousness avoidance of desire, turning the wording into a comprehensive maxim that includes pilgrimage rites and pardon.
rows.anchor: المراد بالبر متابعة الأمر مطلقا وبالتقوى اجتناب الهوى لتصير الآية من جوامع الكلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The source links all pilgrimage rites to God-consciousness and includes pardon within the general maxim.
rows.anchor: جميع مناسك الحج فقد قال تعالى : فانها من تقوى القلوب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The prohibition on cooperating in sin and aggression is also general, covering every form of injustice and disobedience, including assistance in assault and retaliation.
rows.anchor: فيعم النهى كل ماهو من مقولة الظلم والمعاصى ويندرج فيه النهى عن التعاون على الاعتداء والانتقام

rows.speaker: ابن عباس، أبو العالية
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās and Abū al-ʿĀliya explain sin as neglecting commands and committing prohibitions, and aggression as exceeding the limits God set in religion and obligation.
rows.anchor: فسرا الاثم بترك ماأمرهم به وارتكاب مانهاهم عنه والعدوان بمجاوزة ماحده سبحانه لعباده فى دينهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The positive command to adorn conduct with righteousness precedes the negative command to clear it of sin, hastening the demand for the primary purpose.
rows.anchor: وقدمت التحلية على التخلية مسارعة إلى إيجاب ماهو المقصود بالذات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Fear God” covers every matter, including disobeying these commands and prohibitions, and establishes the obligation to fear Him through a demonstrative argument.
rows.anchor: أمر بالاتقاء فى جميع الأمور التى من جملتها مخالفة ماذكر من الأوامر والنواهى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The warning that God is severe in punishment explains the preceding commands; the explicit divine name underscores the point made earlier.
rows.anchor: لمن لايتقيه وهذا فى موضع التعليل لما قبله وإظهار الاسم الجليل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage begins detailing permitted things after the preceding account of prohibitions.
rows.anchor: شروع فى تفصيل المحللات التى ذكر بعضها على وجه الاجمال اثر بيان المحرمات

rows.speaker: أبو رافع
rows.claim: Abū Rāfiʿ reports that Gabriel delayed entering because a house contained an image or dog; after a puppy was found, the Prophet ordered dogs killed in Medina, and people’s question about what remained lawful occasioned the verse.
rows.anchor: أخرج ابن جرير والبيهقى فى سننه وغيرهما عن أبى رافع قال : جاء جبريل عليه السلام

rows.speaker: عكرمة
rows.claim: ʿIkrima identifies the questioners as ʿĀṣim ibn ʿAdī, Saʿd ibn Khaythama, and ʿUwaym ibn Sāʿida.
rows.anchor: وأخرج ابن جرير عن عكرمة أن السائل عاصم بن عدى وسعد بن خيثمة وعويم بن ساعدة

rows.speaker: ابن جبير
rows.claim: Ibn Jubayr instead names ʿAdī ibn Ḥātim and Zayd ibn al-Muhalhil al-Ṭāʾī as the questioners.
rows.anchor: وأخرج ابن أبى حاتم عن ابن جبير أن السائل عدى بن حاتم وزيد بن المهلهل الطائيان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The question embeds the meaning of a statement, so its answer is quoted as a clause; the verb governs the clause because asking causes and leads to knowledge, contrary to Abū Ḥayyān.
rows.anchor: وقد ضمن السؤال معنى القول ولذا حكيت به الجملة كما تحكى بالقول وليس معلقا

rows.speaker: أبو حيان
rows.claim: Abū Ḥayyān disagrees that the question verb can govern the clause; some grammarians posit an omitted noun, “the answer to what was made lawful.”
rows.anchor: خلافا لأبى حيان فاندفع ماقيل : إن السؤال ليس مما يعمل فى الجمل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The prior context suggests they ask which foods and meals are permitted; another view takes the question to concern game and slaughter.
rows.anchor: المسئول نظرا للكلام السابق ماأحل من المطاعم والمآكل

rows.speaker: البلخي
rows.claim: Al-Balkhī defines wholesome things as those that sound human dispositions do not find disgusting or recoil from.
rows.anchor: مالم تستخبثه الطباع السليمة ولم تنفر عنه وإلى ذلك ذهب البلخى

rows.speaker: أبو علي الجبائي، أبو مسلم
rows.claim: Abū ʿAlī al-Jubbāʾī and Abū Muslim define wholesome things as foods, sacrifices, and game God has authorized people to eat.
rows.anchor: وعن أبى على الجبائى وأبى مسلم هى ماأذن سبحانه فى أكله من المأكولات والذبائح والصيد

rows.speaker: قائلون
rows.claim: Another definition is anything for which no text or analogy establishes a prohibition; consensus also falls within this view because it must rest on textual evidence.
rows.anchor: مالم يرد بتحريمه نص أو قياس ويدخل فى ذلك الاجماع إذ لابد من استناده لنص

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On the latter two definitions “wholesome” means lawful, while on the first it means pleasant; Arabic usage supports both senses.
rows.anchor: والطيب على هذين القولين بمعنى الحلال وعلى الأول بمعنى الحلال وعلى الأول بمعنى المستلذ وقد جاء بالمعنيين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One grammatical analysis coordinates “what you train” with wholesome things as a relative clause, supplying an omitted “catch”; another treats it as the source of catching, a specific case under the general permission.
rows.anchor: عطف على الطيبات بتقدير مضاف على أن ما موصولة والعائد محذوف أى وصيد ماعلمتموه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ālūsī says the apparent reading needs no implied “catch,” because permissibility and prohibition attach to actions.
rows.anchor: الظاهر أنه لاحاجة إلى جعل الصيد لأن الحل والحرمة مما يتعلق بالفعل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, “what” is conditional and the following command is its response, coordinated with the sentence “the wholesome things are made lawful for you.”
rows.anchor: ويحتمل أن تكون ما شرطية مبتدأ والجواب فكلوا والخبر الجواب والشرط على المختار

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī allows an implied noun even with conditional “what,” since a noun annexed to a conditional expression has the same grammatical status as the expression itself.
rows.anchor: ونقل عن الزمخشرى أنه قال بالتقدير فيه وقال تقديره لايبطل كون ما شرطية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The implied-noun analysis is challenged because the predicate would then need an understood referent, unless “what they caught” is made to stand in place of “what you trained.”
rows.anchor: وتعقب بأنه على ذلك التقدير يصير الخبر حاليا عن ضمير المبتدأ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A further, less apparent analysis treats “what” as a relative pronoun and “eat” as its predicate, with the prefixed faʾ inserted by analogy to a conditional clause.
rows.anchor: وجوز كونها مبتدأ على تقدير كونها موصولة أيضا والخبر كلوا والفاء إنما دخلت تشبيها للموصول باسم الشرط

rows.speaker: أبو البقاء
rows.claim: Abū al-Baqāʾ takes the hāʾ in “jawāriḥ” as an intensive feminine ending; the word is commonly used without an expressed noun.
rows.anchor: الجوارح حمع جارحة والهاء فيها كا قال أبو البقاء للمبالغة وهى صفة غلبة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Jawāriḥ” means acquisitive beasts of prey and birds, either because they earn for their owners or because they commonly wound prey.
rows.anchor: الكواسب من سباع البهائم والطير وهو من قولهم

rows.speaker: ابن عمر، السدي، الضحاك، أئمة أهل البيت
rows.claim: Ibn ʿUmar, al-Suddī, al-Ḍaḥḥāk, and a report ascribed to the Imams of the Prophet’s family restrict “jawāriḥ” to dogs.
rows.anchor: وعن ابن عمر رضى الله تعالى عنهما والسدى والضحاك وهو المروى عن أئمة أهل البيت بزعم الشيعة أنها الكلاب فقط

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Mukallibīn” means training the hunting animals; the term derives from the dog because it is commonly trained, or because every beast of prey may be called a dog.
rows.anchor: أى معلمين لها الصيد والمكلب مؤدب الجوارح ومضربها بالصيد

rows.speaker: أبو نوفل
rows.claim: Abū Nawfal reports that a lion killed Lahab ibn Abī Lahab after the Prophet prayed for a “dog” to be set upon him; al-Ḥākim graded the report sound in chain, though al-Ālūsī says it does not show birds are included.
rows.anchor: صحيح الأسناد من حديث أبى نوفل قال : كان لهب بن أبى لهب يسب النبى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another etymology derives “mukallibīn” from kalb meaning avidity: someone may be called avid for something, and the participle describes the trainer.
rows.anchor: من الكلب الذى هو بمعنى الضرواة يقال : هو كلب بكذا إذا ضاربا به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The circumstantial “mukallibīn” emphasizes the intensity of training, since only an expert at the craft is called a trainer.
rows.anchor: وانتصابه على الحالية من فاعل علمتم وفائدتها المبالغة فى التعليم لما أن الملكب لايقع إلا على النحرير فى علمه

rows.speaker: ابن عباس، ابن مسعود، الحسن
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās, Ibn Masʿūd, and al-Ḥasan read “mukallibīn” with a light consonant from “aklaba”; the forms faʿʿala and afʿala can share a meaning.
rows.anchor: وعن ابن عباس وابن مسعود والحسن رضى الله تعالى عنهم أنهم قرأوا مكلبين بالتخفيف من أكلب وفعل وأفعل قد يستعملان بمعنى واحد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Teaching them” may be circumstantial from the pronoun in “trainers,” an independent sentence if “what” is not conditional, or a second circumstance from “you trained”; Abū al-Baqāʾ’s objection to two circumstances from one governor is questioned.
rows.anchor: حال من ضمير مكلبين أو استئنافية إن لم تكن ما شرطية وإلا فهى معترضة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “From what God taught you” refers to techniques and methods of training, given either by divine inspiration or by the intellect God created in the animals.
rows.anchor: من الحيل وطرق التعليم والتأديب وذلك إما بالالهام منه سبحاته أو بالعقل الذى خلقه فيهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another explanation is that God taught people the signs of trained prey: the animal responds to release and command, returns when called, and holds prey without eating it.
rows.anchor: المراد مما عرفكم سبحانه أن تعلموه من اتباع الصيد بأن يسترسل بارسال صاحبه وينزجر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In “from what God taught you,” the preposition may indicate cause or mean “some of what God taught you.”
rows.anchor: من أجلية وقيل : تبعيضية أى بعض ما علمكم الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Eat what they catch for you” follows from the permission for trained animals, makes explicit the result of training, or serves as a conditional response or predicate.
rows.anchor: جملة متفرعة على بيان حل صيد الجوارح المعلمة مبنية للمضاف المقدر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The preposition in “from what they caught” is partitive because hides, bones, and other parts of a catch are not eaten; al-Akhfash instead treats it as extra.
rows.anchor: من تبعيضية إذ من الممسك مالا يؤكل كالجلد والعظم وغير ذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “What” is relative or descriptive with an omitted object, and the feminine pronoun refers to the trained animals; “for you” is figuratively an expression of superiority.
rows.anchor: ما موصولة أو موصوفة والعائد محذوف أى أمسكنه وضمير الؤنث للجوارح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The restriction “for you” excludes prey the animals catch for themselves, signaled by their eating from it.
rows.anchor: والتقييد بذلك لاخراج ماأمسكنه على أنفسهن وعلامته أن يأكلن منه

rows.speaker: عدي بن حاتم
rows.claim: A report from ʿAdī ibn Ḥātim says that if a trained dog was released in God’s name, one may eat what it catches for its owner, but not if it eats, since then it caught the prey for itself; most jurists follow this.
rows.anchor: روى أصحاب السنن عن عدى بن حاتم

rows.speaker: علي، الشعبي، عكرمة
rows.claim: ʿAlī, al-Shaʿbī, and ʿIkrima are also reported to hold that prey from a dog that eats must not be eaten.
rows.anchor: روى عن على كرم الله تعالى وجهه والشعبى وعكرمة

rows.speaker: أبو حنيفة وأصحابه
rows.claim: Abū Ḥanīfa and his followers say a dog that eats its catch is untrained and its prey is unlawful, but prey from a falcon or similar bird remains lawful even if it eats because such birds cannot be trained not to eat.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو حنيفة رضى الله تعالى عنه وأصحابه إذا أكل الكلب من الصيد فهو غير معلم لايؤكل صيده ويؤكل صيد البازى ونحوه

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās is reported to distinguish dogs from falcons: do not eat prey if the dog eats, but eat prey if the falcon eats, since the dog can be beaten and the falcon cannot.
rows.anchor: إذا أكل الكلب فلا تأكل وإذا أكل الصقر فكل لأن الكلب تستطيع أن تضربه

rows.speaker: إمام الحرمين
rows.claim: Imām al-Ḥaramayn, a Shāfiʿī, follows the distinction that tolerates a hunting bird’s eating its prey.
rows.anchor: وعليه إمام الحرمين من الشافعية

rows.speaker: مالك، الليث
rows.claim: Mālik and al-Layth permit eating the catch even when the dog has eaten from it.
rows.anchor: يؤكل وان أكل الكلب منه وقد روى عن سلمان

rows.speaker: سلمان، سعد بن أبي وقاص، أبو هريرة
rows.claim: Salman, Saʿd ibn Abī Waqqāṣ, and Abū Hurayra are reported to permit the catch if the dog ate two-thirds, a third remains, and God’s name was invoked.
rows.anchor: وقد روى عن سلمان وسعد بن أبى وقاص وأبى هريرة رضى الله تعالى عنهم أنه إذا أكل الكلب ثلثيه وبقى ثلثه

rows.speaker: ابن عباس، الحسن، السدي
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Ḥasan, and al-Suddī take “invoke God’s name over it” to mean saying the name when releasing the trained animal.
rows.anchor: الضمير لما علمتم كما يدل عليه الخبر السابق والمعنى سموا عليه عند إرساله وروى ذلك ابن عباس والحسن والسدى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Others refer the pronoun to the caught animal and say the name if it is found alive and slaughtered; a further, less likely view refers it to the act of eating, as Abū Ḥayyān prefers.
rows.anchor: لما أمسكن أى سموا عليه إذا أدركتم ذكائه

rows.speaker: أبو حنيفة، الشافعي
rows.claim: Abū Ḥanīfa regards invoking God’s name as obligatory, while al-Shāfiʿī regards it as recommended; on the eating-time interpretation, it is recommended by agreement.
rows.anchor: والأمر للوجوب عند أبى حنيفة رضى الله تعالى عنه وللندب عند الشافعى وهو على القول الأخير للندب بالاتفاق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command to fear God concerns His prohibitions, including eating prey caught by untrained animals; “swift in reckoning” means that His accounting comes or is completed swiftly.
rows.anchor: فى شأن محرماته ومنها أكل صيد الجوارح الغير المعلمة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Whether the reckoning begins quickly or is completed quickly, God takes account of every deed, small and great; the explicit divine name builds awe and explains the rule.
rows.anchor: والمراد على التقديرين أنه جل شأنه يؤاخذكم على جميع الأفعال حقيرها وجليلها وإظهار الاسم الجليل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The warning after hunting encourages vigilance because hunting often distracts people from prayer and purity; hunters who guard their religion are rarer than a white crow and are rewarded.
rows.anchor: ذكر هذا إثر بيان حكم الصيد لحث متعاطيه على التقوى لما أنه مظنة التهاون والغفلة

rows.speaker: صفوان بن أمية
rows.claim: In a report from Ṣafwān ibn Umayya, ʿUrfuṭa ibn Nāhik asks whether hunting is lawful for a family dependent on it despite its distraction from remembrance and congregational prayer; the Prophet permits it, calls lawful provision a form of striving, and urges love of the congregation and remembrance.
rows.anchor: الطبرانى عن صفوان بن أمية أن عرفطة بن نهيك التميمى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse supports teaching animals and striking them when useful, as well as keeping dogs for hunting; guard dogs are included by analogy.
rows.anchor: واستدل بالآية على جواز تعليم الحيوان وضربه للمصلحة لأن التعليم قد يحتاج لذلك وعلى إباحة اتخاذ الكلب للصيد

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says game caught by a Magian’s trained dog, hawk, falcon, or eagle is not lawful even with invocation, because the animal was trained by a Magian rather than through God’s teaching.
rows.anchor: إلى هذا ذهب ابن عباس رضى الله تعالى عنهما فقد روى عنه فى المسلم يأخذ كلب المجوسى
